For an example "the world is gray. Color the world by walking over surfaces" is not really the use of colours as it's more an effect than a mechanic. Combining lights and mirrors is something more like it this one uses colours as a mechanic. But is there a game that makes even more clever use of colours to integrate into gameplay?
[Discussion] What games have made a great use of colours as a gameplay mechanic?

Mirror's Edge, somewhat.

The game had a very distinct art style, a very "clean", sterile atmosphere with tons of whites and blues in its color palette. The color red fit very well in that palette, but it was used exclusively to guide the player's path and to highlight objects the player could use to progress. It wasn't used for anything else other than textures on the main character and general menu / main screen / disc cover / PR artwork, where it had a very defining and iconic role, and hence it never felt out of place in-game, but it was pretty much entirely limited to guiding the player and not used for any other elements.
Turgor/ The Void had heavy symbolism in its colors, but it's a game that really isn't for anyone.
I loved that Mario game with the water jet, where you had to clean paint off of everything. Suoer Mario Sunshine or Paradise? I don't think a lot of others liked that game, though.

The puzzle game PiCTOBiTS on DSiWare is the first one that comes to mind for me. It's a little hard to explain, so let me link a trailer instead:

Q.U.B.E used colour as a mechanic; Primarily as a visual aid. Coloured platforms react because of coloured blocks.

Bit.Trip Runner reminds me of a japanese arcade game, where the screen gets more colourful, along with the audio effects, to encourage the player.
Bit.Trip's mechanics do not have anything to do with colours itself. It's more of a game feedback.

Splinter Cell: Conviction had this great game mechanic that transitioned your screen to black and white when you were concealed. It was an unobtrusive way to let you know how hidden you were and it started to blend with the other game mechanics to almost be a "sixth sense" while playing.

I vaguely remember that now that you mention it, and I love stuff like that, integrating the art style / visuals with gameplay mechanics. In this case double so because of how unobtrusive the effect is and how it becomes so intuitive right away. This is great on so many levels, and a lot of people probably don't even appreciate the ingenuity of that mechanic, mostly because it's so well implemented that people don't even spend any time thinking about it.
I think that's the perfect way to put it. Some innovations are so well implemented that you don't even notice them, or quickly forget they're there.
